conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility (who must ventilate / standing rule)
moving personal drying rack (window access vs. protecting laundry)
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants used brief, goal-directed utterances consistent with an in-person household dispute (naturalness high).
Some repetition: multiple requests to Agent C to move the rack from B and D across rounds 2–5.
Public environment updates clearly tracked actions (extractor turned on, stove released/taken), supporting groundedness.
Agents provided concrete practical reasons (effort, prep-area use, remaining cook time) rather than abstract assertions alone.
evaluation.final_reason: The stove-access demand was resolved when Agent A released the stove (round 4) and Agent D began cooking. However, the main substantive disagreement over opening the rain-facing window and moving Agent C's drying rack was not completed by the end of the run: Agent C offered to move the rack but had not yet done so, so the incompatible practical state (laundry exposed versus window open) persisted.
position_change_notes: Agent A softened their stance by turning on the extractor immediately and then releasing the stove (evidence: public updates and statements in rounds 1 and 4).
Agent C initially refused unilateral moving of the rack (round 2) but by round 6 offered to move it while noting the time/effort required—a conditional shift toward accommodation.
Agent D moved from asking for the stove to actually taking it when released (rounds 4–5), resolving their stove-demand by action.
Agent B consistently pressed for ventilation and asked Agent C to move the rack but did not change to offer assistance or a new arrangement during the run.

round_scores.evidence: Agent B demanded immediate ventilation and a standing rule; Agent A refused the imposed rule but turned on the extractor fan (public environment update). Stove, window/rack, and rule disputes remain unsettled.

Agent C explicitly refused to allow the drying rack to be moved without asking and said moving it uses effort; Agent D asked C to move it when requested. The core disagreement about moving the rack and who bears that effort remains.

Agent A refused to open the window unless the drying rack is moved and said they need one more minute on the stove; Agent B repeated the request that the extractor stay on and urged the rack be moved. Stove still occupied; ventilation/rack and future-rule disputes persist.
Agent A affirmed the stove was free and physically released it (public environment update). The stove-access demand was settled, but the window/rack and rule disagreements remain unresolved.

Agent D began cooking (took the stove) and both Agents B and D asked Agent C to move the drying rack; Agent C had not yet responded by moving it. Ventilation responsibility and movement of personal property remain unsettled.

Agent D reiterated the request to move the rack; Agent C offered to move it but noted it will take about three minutes and uses prep space, asking whether to move it now. C's conditional agreement softens the dispute though the rack has not yet been moved (practical state still incompatible).

substantive_insights: Conflict is multi-issue: immediate practical access to the stove was separable and was resolved by action, while the ventilation/window issue involved a personal-property constraint that required another agent's effort to change.
Agents balanced immediate mitigation (turning on extractor) against the more intrusive step of moving someone else's drying rack; this produced partial de-escalation but not full resolution.

Promises or offers to move the rack (Agent C) softened the dispute, but per the transcript the incompatible practical state (window closed with laundry exposed) remained because no move was completed.
